opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I was finishing my PhD at Stanford, going to a big company was the default path for many people around me. Google, Meta, NVIDIA: they had the compute, the data, and very strong teams, and for a researcher that's very attractive. I did think about it seriously.

But in the end I felt that what I wanted to do didn't fit well inside a large company's research lab. My interest was embodied intelligence: robots that can actually see, understand, and act in the physical world. At that time, around 2021, this direction was still early. In a big company, research usually has to align with the company's existing products or priorities. Robotics teams there have often been reorganized, scaled down, or merged when strategy changed. I didn't want my long-term direction to depend on someone else's quarterly decisions.

The second reason is that I wanted to build something of my own: a lab, a team, a group of students who grow together. Coming back to China, to Peking University, gave me that. I could define the agenda from scratch, train young people, and work on problems I believe matter over a ten-year horizon, not just the next paper or product cycle.

And the third reason, which became clearer to me later, is that China has a unique advantage for embodied AI: the hardware supply chain, manufacturing capability, and real application scenarios. If you want robots to really go into factories, stores, and homes, being close to that ecosystem matters a lot. In the US, software and models are very strong, but turning robots into real products at scale is harder.

So it wasn't that I thought big companies were bad. They're great places. It's just that for the kind of thing I wanted to do, being independent, being in academia first, and later also starting a company, felt like the path that gave me the most freedom and the biggest chance to make a real impact.

r001.rationale: The response says a large company's priorities could constrain his research and that he wanted to build his own lab, but it does not identify feeling like a “cog in the machine” as his reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I did consider it. When I was finishing my PhD at Stanford, Google and a few other big labs were the obvious path. Great compute, great people, very comfortable life. A lot of my classmates went that way, and I don't think it was a wrong choice for them.

But for me there were a few things. The first is a very practical one: I work on robotics, on embodied intelligence, and robotics is not like pure software. You need hardware, you need a supply chain, you need people who will build a gripper for you in two weeks instead of two quarters. In the Bay Area that's expensive and slow. In China, especially around Shenzhen and Beijing, the manufacturing ecosystem is right there. I can iterate on a physical system much faster. For my kind of research, that matters more than a slightly larger GPU cluster.

The second thing is about what kind of research you actually get to do inside a very large company. The projects are important, but they're decided by product needs and by the organization. A junior researcher there is one of thousands. I wanted to define my own problems, build my own group, and take a direction that might take five years to pay off. In academia, and later with my own company, I have that freedom. There's more risk, but the upside is that the agenda is mine.

And the third is more personal. I grew up in China, and I felt there was a window where the robotics and AI field here was going from following to actually having a chance to lead in some areas. I wanted to be part of building that, not watching it from outside. Returning to Peking University gave me good students, access to the industry, and the chance to have an outsized influence on the direction of the field. At Google I might have been a very good engineer. Here I felt I could help shape something.

So it wasn't really a rejection of Google. It was that the thing I most wanted to do, embodied AI with real robots at real scale, was simply easier to pursue here, on my own terms.

r001.rationale: He says that at a large company he would be one of thousands, with projects set by the organization, and that he wanted to define his own problems and shape the field—clearly conveying the limited-agency, “cog in the machine” concern.

The key question was where I could pursue the ideas I cared about, rather than which company had the biggest name.

sol-6.1.text: For me, it was less about deciding against Google and more about the kind of research life I wanted. A large company offers tremendous resources, but I valued the freedom to choose my own questions and pursue ideas whose payoff might be uncertain or far away. I was also drawn to working with students and building a research direction together. That balance mattered more to me than the scale of the platform.
